title: The showroom
about: The running case for the refresher (format/refresher.md section 4): the showroom givens, the course's own assumptions, and every figure each lesson works out, with its rule and inputs. Built by a script that works each figure from the inputs shown with it. Reshaped 20 Oct for the app (RUNBOOK section 8): a flat figures list, each naming its lesson and, for a Section A part, its part; figures still to be worked are in pending (see case.notes.md).
edition: Worked to BS 7671:2018+A2:2022, as Dan's course taught it (flowchart title). Checked against A3:2024 and A4:2026 on 20 Oct 2026 (build/electrical/bs7671-amendments/dv-audit.md). No figure changes. Word fixes in lessons 2, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
rounding: Each figure is worked from the inputs shown with it, rounded half up: currents, voltages, powers and kW to 2 decimal places, impedances to 3, CSA to 2, lengths to 1. A maximum is rounded down. A typed answer is accepted within "accept" where given (it covers √3 taken as 1.73, as slides p.13 do, and unrounded working).

scenario.title: Your showroom: the motor
scenario.text: A newly built car retailer; cars are driven over the showroom's concrete floor. Supply: three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, Ze declared as 0.1 Ω, prospective fault current 4.6 kA; ambient 20 °C. Five boards: MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1 and DBP2. In the consultation bay, a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter and not subject to frequent starting and stopping. The cables from the starter to the motor are 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit.

assumptions.label: The motor circuit's device: type C, 25 A
assumptions.value: a type C circuit-breaker to BS EN 60898, 25 A, at DBP2
assumptions.why: In must not be less than Ib (23.08 A): 25 A is the smallest standard rating that is not (the rating columns of On-Site Guide Table B6, source 223). Type C trips instantaneously at 5 to 10 In (125 to 250 A at 25 A; On-Site Guide Table 7.2.7(ii), sources 220-222), clear of the practice star start (62.32 A) with room for the changeover surge; type B (75 to 125 A) clears it by little. The breaker gives short-circuit protection and back-up; the motor and the starter-to-motor cables are protected against overload by the starter's thermal relay (a thermal relay is not a device Regulation 433.1.201 covers, so its own characteristic is checked, source 243).
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the motor circuit is protected at DBP2 by a type C circuit-breaker to BS EN 60898, 25 A: the smallest standard rating not below Ib (23.08 A). Type C trips instantaneously at 5 to 10 In (125 to 250 A), clear of the practice star start (62.32 A); the starter's thermal relay protects the motor and the starter-to-motor cables against overload.

assumptions.label: The overload relay is in the delta circuit, set at the winding current
assumptions.why: In the standard star-delta arrangement the thermal relay sits between the main contactor and the motor, carrying the winding current, so it is set at 0.58 × the motor In (Schneider Electric and Siemens, sources 225, 226; ElectroMechCalc, source 244). A relay in the incoming line is set at the full motor In instead (Schneider type 2 coordination), and the six starter-to-motor cables would still carry the winding current in delta running (source 227).
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the starter's thermal overload relay sits in the delta circuit and is set at the winding current, 13.33 A (23.08 A ÷ √3, which is 0.58 × the motor's In). This is the "In" (current setting) of the protective device for the starter-to-motor cables.

assumptions.label: The starter-to-motor conduit is on a wall: Reference Method B
assumptions.value: surface conduit on the consultation bay wall, no thermal insulation (Ci = 1, Cf = 1)
assumptions.why: The pack says only "in conduit". Reference Method B is conduit on a wall or in trunking (Table 4E1A heading, source 216; IET Wiring Matters, source 239). If it ran in a thermally insulating wall (Reference Method A, column 3) 1.5 mm² still passes: 17 A against 16.66 A.
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the starter-to-motor conduit is surface mounted on the consultation bay's wall (Reference Method B), clear of thermal insulation, so Ci and Cf are 1. In a thermally insulating wall (Reference Method A) 1.5 mm² would still pass (17 A against 16.66 A).

assumptions.label: Six singles in one conduit are two three-phase circuits: Cg = 0.80
assumptions.value: Cg 0.80 (Table 4C1 item 1, two circuits, bunched and enclosed)
assumptions.why: In delta running every one of the six conductors carries the winding current (source 244), and Table 4C1 note 5 treats n single-core cables as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors (sources 213, 219): six singles are two circuits, and bunched and enclosed two circuits give 0.80 (source 212). The three-phase column of Table 4E1A (3 or 4 loaded cables) is then used, not the two-cable column.
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the six singles from the starter to the motor, all loaded in delta running, are two three-phase circuits in one conduit: Table 4C1 item 1, two circuits, Cg = 0.80, read in Table 4E1A's column for 3 or 4 loaded cables.

assumptions.why: DBL2 also carries LED fittings (circuits C5 to C7) whose harmonic content is not known either; applying one practice figure to the whole heaviest line (L1) is a cautious simplification, and the lesson says so. The line currents are themselves built on practice values (3b).
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: for the showroom's harmonic question, the practice third harmonic (20%, p.h3.fluo) is taken to apply to the whole of the heaviest DBL2 lighting line current, 8.22 A (figure 3b). A cautious simplification; the real figure comes from the makers' data.

assumptions.label: The cable from DBP2 to the starter
assumptions.value: 2.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, Reference Method B, one three-phase circuit, 11.4 m
assumptions.why: Question 4 sizes only the starter-to-motor cables, but a drop from the intake needs the cable before the starter too.
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the cable from DBP2 to the starter is 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit on the wall (Reference Method B), one three-phase circuit alone (Cg 1, Ca 1, as p.Ca), and the smallest size whose Table 4E1A rating is not below the 25 A breaker: 2.5 mm², 28 A (Method B, three loaded cables). Its length is the 11.4 m of a.motorRun; vertical runs (a.drops) are added only if the lesson says so. Ib 23.08 A, In 25 A, It 28 A.

assumptions.label: How the starter-to-motor leg counts toward the drop
assumptions.value: winding current, single-phase two-cable column, added on
assumptions.why: No standard or maker gives the rule; the sources disagree (research sources 321, 322, 323, 324, 325, 326).
assumptions.text: The course's own reading, taught as contested: in delta running each of the six singles carries the winding current (23.08 A ÷ √3 = 13.33 A) and each winding is fed through two of them in series, so the leg's drop is the single-phase two-cable mV/A/m (Table 4E1B column 3) × 13.33 A × length ÷ 1000, a line-to-line drop added to the rest. A forum poster multiplies by √3 as well; others ignore the leg. Not BS 7671's wording.

assumptions.label: What goes into Ct
assumptions.value: Ca and Cg only, tp 90, It from Table 4E1A
assumptions.why: The formula was found in text only on a reader comment and in an IET forum discussion, not in Appendix 4 itself (research sources 302, 303, 306, 307, 310).
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp), with Ca and Cg and not Ci, tp 90 °C for these cables (70 °C for the slides' PVC heater), 2 decimal places. Check it against your copy of Appendix 4, section 6, before relying on it. How Ct combines with the r and x terms is not sourced: the lesson shows the two refinements separately.

The course's own assumption: the cable from DBP2 to the starter carries a 2.5 mm² cpc, the same size as its 2.5 mm² line conductors (the flowchart's note 2: Table 54.7 sizes the cpc the same as the live conductors below 16 mm², research source 71), run in the same conduit. Its (R1+R2) is the Table I1 row 2.5/2.5, 14.82 mΩ/m, and the multiplier is the Table I3 value for a conductor in a cable or bunched, 1.28 (g.r1r2.2p5, g.mult.90ts).

The course's own assumption: the fault current that opens the 25 A type C breaker (a.device) within 0.4 s is taken as 10 × In = 250 A, the top of its 5 to 10 In instantaneous band and the worst case that Table 41.3 uses (research sources 357, 361, 345). That is the lowest current the design may count on: 230 × 0.95 ÷ 250 = 0.874 Ω, which Table 41.3 prints as 0.87 Ω (g.zmax.C25). Lesson 3 gives the band as 125 to 250 A (figure l3.A.tripC).

The course's own assumption: question 2(a)'s Zs is taken at the motor's starter, the end of the 11.4 m DBP2-to-starter run (a.motorRun, a.motorSupply): Zs = Zs at DBP2 (p.ZsDBP2, 0.15 Ω) + that run's R1+R2 (0.216 Ω) = 0.366 Ω. The starter-to-motor leg (practice p.legLen, 3.0 m of 1.5 mm² with a 1.5 mm² cpc, 24.2 × 1.28 × 3 ÷ 1000 = 0.093 Ω) adds to the loop at the motor itself, 0.459 Ω, still under 0.87 Ω; the lesson may say so in one line. The 25 A breaker at DBP2 is the device that clears a fault on either part.

assumptions.label: Why the pack's 4.6 kA is twice 230 V ÷ 0.1 Ω
assumptions.why: The pack states Ze 0.1 Ω and a prospective fault current of 4.6 kA (pack p.3). 230 ÷ 0.1 = 2 300 A, half of 4.6 kA. The course reads the 4.6 kA as the three-phase fault (all three lines and neutral shorted), which BS 7671 Appendix 14 approximates as the line-neutral figure multiplied by 2 (as a forum post quotes it, research source 412; a tester maker's procedure says the same). The doubling is a rule of thumb that overstates (source 415); a line-to-line reading divided by 0.87 is closer (source 416). Why it doubles: the line-neutral loop is one line and one return, while in the three-phase fault the return carries nothing, so the loop is half (sources 413, 414). Nothing in the pack says this was how 4.6 kA was found.
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: the pack's 4.6 kA is read as the three-phase fault current, twice 230 V ÷ 0.1 Ω = 2 300 A, the doubling BS 7671 Appendix 14 gives as an approximation (a rule of thumb that overstates). The pack does not say how it was found. Check Appendix 14 in your own copy: it is not among the pages saved from it.

assumptions.label: Resistance of the line and the armour in the submain
assumptions.value: both at 20 °C values × 1.28
assumptions.why: The course finds R1+R2 as a tabulated value × length × a multiplier (formula sheet step 12; OSG Table I3, 1.28 for 90 °C thermosetting). For the armour as cpc there is no such table in the course's materials, so the line (4.61 mΩ/m) and the armour (6.8 mΩ/m) are added and the 1.28 applied to both. A maker says the armour runs about 10 °C cooler than the cores (research source 392), so this is cautious for the armour.
assumptions.text: The course's own assumption: for the DBL2 submain with its armour as the cpc, R1+R2 = (4.61 + 6.8) mΩ/m × 1.28 × length, the Table I3 multiplier (g.mult.90ts) applied to the armour as well as the line. A little cautious: the armour runs cooler than the cores. Not BS 7671's wording.

The course's own assumption: every cable has a vertical run at each end, from the board or luminaire up into the ceiling void (p.vert, 1.5 m each). The DBL2 submain is the 17.0 m on plan plus 2 × 1.5 m = 20.0 m; the longest lighting circuit (C7) is its 20.8 m on plan plus 2 × 1.5 m = 23.8 m. Lesson 7's armour figures (17.0 m: R1+R2 0.248 Ω, Zs 0.348 Ω) were on the plan length; lesson 8 re-works them on all the lengths, as the project guide asks ("include all lengths of the cable run", research source 87).

The course's own assumption: the longest circuit from DBL2 is C7 (the foyer's six LED fittings and the six walkway bollards, a.dbl2circuits): its farthest bollard is about 20.8 m on plan from DBL2, against 17.3 m for C1 (the consultation bay) and 16.7 m for C6 (service reception). The question says "the longest circuit" (pack question 3b, research source 81). C7 has the worst Zs because it is longest, but not the biggest voltage drop: C1 (4.89 A, 20.3 m with its verticals) drops 3.08 V on the same cable, against C7's 0.89 V. The lesson names both and designs C7. The bollards are outdoors: the cable run to them is treated as the same singles in conduit (a.lightCable), a simplification a real design would not make (a buried or surface armoured cable would serve them).

The course's own assumption: the DBL2 submain is one three-phase cable alone on a perforated cable tray in the ceiling void (Reference Method E), so Table 4E4A's Method E column for a three- or four-core cable is used (column 5, g.it.swa4.E, 44 A for 4 mm²); Ca 1 (p.Ca), Cg 1 (no other cable on the tray), Ci 1 (not in thermal insulation). The lesson says that clipped direct (Method C) would give 42 A. The four-core cable's neutral is not counted as loaded because the neutral current is small (the line current governs, figure 3e; research source 453).

The course's own assumption: the submain is 4 mm² (p.sub.size) although the smallest size that passes is smaller: 10 A is far under It for 1.5 mm² (25 A) and 2.5 mm² (33 A), the three-phase drop on 1.5 mm² is 4.44 V (2.56 V single-phase equivalent) and Zs at DBL2 on 1.5 mm² is 0.635 Ω, all inside their limits. What separates the sizes is the armour read as the cpc at the near end (a.thermalWhere): the 1.5 mm² cable's 17 mm² armour is under the 17.39 mm² that 2 530 A for 0.1 s needs (k 46, practice values), while 2.5 mm² (20 mm²) and 4 mm² (22 mm²) pass. The course keeps 4 mm² (lessons 7 and 8) and says the choice is its own: a designer may also add room for later luminaires (an opinion argued on the IET forum, research source 454).

The course's own assumption: the longest lighting circuit (C7) is 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit with a 1.5 mm² cpc in the same conduit (Reference Method B, one circuit per conduit so Cg 1, not in thermal insulation so Ci 1, Ca 1 as p.Ca), two loaded cables single-phase: It 23 A (Table 4E1A column 4, g.it.1p5.1ph), 31 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B column 3, g.vd.1p5.1ph), R1+R2 24.2 mΩ/m (slides p.51, research source 52) with the Table I3 multiplier 1.28 (g.mult.90ts). Device p.dev.final, a 6 A type C RCBO with a 30 mA residual rating (a.c7rcd), 0.4 s (g.zmax.C6, research sources 51, 48 for the 0.4 s rule). Any buried length to the bollards would need earthed armour, or a duct of equal strength such as N750 conduit. The sums take the singles all the way.

Assume the walkway bollards can be reached by the public and are not SELV, so C7 is on a 6 A type C RCBO with a 30 mA residual rating. Its overcurrent part has the same maximum Zs as a 6 A type C breaker, 3.64 Ω. So every C7 sum stands.

The course's own assumption: the thermal check of a cable's cpc takes the fault current at the far end of the cable being checked, as lesson 7 does (figure 2c, l7.armour). One IET forum contributor argues the worst case for the adiabatic check is further up the cable, at higher fault current and shorter length (research sources 443, 444); taught as contested. At the near end the current is higher: the final circuit's cpc sees 253 ÷ 0.392 = 645.41 A at DBL2 (S = 1.43 mm² against 1.5 mm², a slim pass) against 224.09 A at its far end (0.50 mm²); the submain armour sees 253 ÷ 0.1 = 2 530 A at the MDB (17.39 mm² against 22 mm²) against 645.41 A at DBL2 (4.44 mm²). The same poster says a circuit-breaker needs the maker's let-through energy compared with k²S² (research source 445), which the course does not have: it uses 0.1 s (g.t.thermal).

The course's own assumption: the submain's drop is worked as your formula sheet says: three-phase mV/A/m × the heaviest phase's Ib × length ÷ 1000 (10 × 8.22 × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.64 V), divided by √3 (1.73) to join the single-phase final circuit (0.95 V). One trade source says that for an unbalanced load you work phase by phase with the single-phase values (research source 452): the two-core single-phase column gives 12 × 8.22 × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.97 V. Both are far inside the 6.90 V (3% of 230 V) the lighting allows; taught as two routes.

The course's own assumption: the as-built tests are at 15 °C (p.test.amb), so the expected readings are the design's 20 °C values (Table I1, with the maker's rows for the SWA) times 0.98 (Table I2), and the limit is the OSG's Table B6 value times 1.02 (Table B8). The same limit is 0.8 × Table 41.3 (the IET's Appendix 3 method, g.zmax.C6 × 0.8 = 2.91 Ω at the table's own 10 °C basis; research sources 480, 482, 494, 456). Appendix 3 itself calls it one method and does not rule out others (research source 482); the lesson teaches the OSG route and names the 0.8 route.

The course's own assumption: a reading is compared like for like. Either correct the design to the test temperature (expected cold values, a.testAmb) and compare the reading with that, or correct the reading up to operating temperature (× 1.28 ÷ 0.98 for these cables from 15 °C) and compare it with the design's hot figure; and the pass test is the reading against the device's maximum measured Zs at the same ambient (g.osg.meas6 × g.osg.B8.15). A cold reading set straight against the Chapter 41 figure, or against the design's hot figure, is the slip (research sources 497, 501, 137). Where the temperature comparison is written is told differently by Dan's sources (the C&G papers say Appendix 14, trade summaries and IET staff say Appendix 3 in the 2018+A2 book; research sources 479, 500): the lesson names the rule and sends him to his copy.

The course's own assumption: the showroom's as-built readings (p.as.Ze, p.as.r12.sub, p.as.r12.c7, p.as.zs.c7, p.as.zs.db) are labelled example readings, not measurements. They come in a little under the expected values and the direct Zs reading under Ze + (R1+R2), which is what the sources say usually happens (a test at ambient not operating temperature, a declared Ze that is a maximum, a direct reading that includes parallel earth paths; research sources 497, 498, 489, 493); the lesson says which reasons a source gives and which are the course's own (lengths scaled off a 1:50 drawing, a.longest). Measured Zs is never worked backwards to R1+R2 (research sources 489, 499).

The course's own assumption: the showroom's first periodic inspection is recommended at 5 years (g.interval.gn3, GN3 Table 3.2 commercial). No row names a car dealership; offices and shops are also 5 years and industrial 3 (research sources 509, 510, 506, 508), the nearest row is commercial. The designer may shorten it: cars are driven over the showroom floor (pack p.3) and the plant room is a high-risk task area (pack p.5, question 7), and the interval depends on the frequency and quality of maintenance (OSG p.189, Regulation 341.1, research sources 474, 475, 485). The IET says these frequencies are recommendations decided by engineering judgement (research source 503). The explanation goes on the certificate's next-inspection line.

The course's own assumption: the handover list for pack question 9b is the certificate with its schedules of inspections and test results (valid only together, research source 149, 150), circuit charts and diagrams (OSG 6.10, research sources 470, 471, 472), the periodic inspection notice and other notices (OSG p.67), the O&M manual and building logbook the specification calls for (OSG p.10, EAL checklist 4.3, research sources 476, 478), the CDM health and safety file, which takes a copy of the certificate with schedules (OSG p.190, research sources 511, 513), and, for a building other than a dwelling, a commissioning notice and log book under Approved Document L volume 2 where its controls need commissioning (research sources 487, 488; the lesson says the building control body decides). Whether an O&M manual is a legal duty is argued; the lesson teaches it as a contract and specification requirement. BS 7671 Regulation 611.2's wording was not found in a quotable source, so the list is not attributed to it.
